I demoed at Photon Residency Demo Day yesterday. 100+ builders in the room. 6 residents. 1 week of building. Before the demo, I thought the hard part was going to be the product: The idea. The code. The agents. The edge cases. The pitch. But once I got in the room, I realized the real value of demo day wasn’t just showing what I built. It was meeting the people who cared enough to show up. Founders. Creators. GTM leads. Engineers from OpenAI, NVIDIA, Anthropic, and Meta. People building at the edge of AI and consumer. Every conversation reminded me why being in the right room matters. You can spend weeks building alone and convince yourself the product is the whole game. Then you demo in front of people who ask the right questions, challenge your assumptions, and make the project feel 10x more real. That was Photon Demo Day for me. A room full of people who didn’t just watch demos. They made the builders better. Grateful to Photon for the residency, the community, and the chance to build alongside so many high-agency people this week. I came in wanting to build something cool with AI. I left realizing the best demos don’t just show what you made. They show you who you’re becoming. ...more

I came into Photon Residency thinking I was here to learn about AI, agents, and coding. And I did. But that wasn’t the biggest thing I took away. The real lesson was people. Before coming to SF, I thought the fastest way to grow was simple: Build better products. Write better code. Delve deeper into agents. But this week reminded me that building is only half the game. The other half is distribution. Being around founders, creators, and people who think out loud made me realize how undervalued the content creator space in SF still is. Content isn’t just posting. It’s how people find your ideas. It’s how trust compounds. It’s how the right people end up in the same room. Photon gave me the technical environment I came for. But it also exposed me to people who made me think bigger about what it means to build in public. Grateful for the people that gave me this new perspective: Noah Kostesku , Ameya Lambat , Sarah Fan , Cecilia Zeng , Winnie Chen , Julie C. , Pavan Kumar , Kelsey Wu -- thank you for making this week what it was! I came to Photon to learn how to build with AI. I left realizing the people you build around shape what you become. ...more

Agentic systems introduce a problem that no one has solved (yet). Traditional software follows clearly defined rules. When something breaks, the failure is usually loud and obvious. Tests fail, exceptions get thrown, or an HTTP request returns anything but 200. An AI system can seemingly execute successfully; meanwhile, your agent made the wrong decision, missed part of a task, or did something you never intended. Nothing has to fail for the behavior to be wrong. This is creating a new challenge with observability. Traditional monitoring is good at telling you when software failed. But agents need a different foundation, one that can tell you when the system ran successfully but the execution path was wrong. That’s what we’re building at Lemma (YC F25) . Catch these silent failures before they reach your users.

Turns out 3 weeks in SF is a lot of life. met people i’d wanted to meet for over a year and said yes to things my past self would’ve normally overthought i think a past version of me would’ve cared a lot about getting to do all of this. being in sf, meeting certain people, going certain places. and it is still cool but when you’re actually living it, none of it feels like some big milestone. it’s just a moment you happen to be in i think the number one thing holding me back for a long time was thinking in a time that didn’t exist we think about the past because it’s comfortable. we use what happened before as evidence for what we should or shouldn’t do now. then we think about the future and convince ourselves there’ll be a better time to try something, say something, go somewhere but the past isn’t here anymore, and the future has never happened there’s a difference between being strategic about your life and thinking about it so much that you forget to actually live it. i’ve been reassured for awhile now that a lot of the best decisions never came from having every variable figured out maybe being present is just learning not to leave a moment before it’s over because eventually the labels, titles and accolades get forgotten anyway the stories stay the random nights, the people you met, the things you tried, the times you went for it when you could’ve simply not done it. those are the things you actually get to keep it was a pleasure sf. see you soon :)

I was invited to YC Startup School last week, and I hated it. Not the event. The event was one of the best things I've ever been invited to. What I hated came the next morning, when I opened LinkedIn and scrolled the same post over and over. Same few famous people, same photo, same caption about how surreal the room was. That bothers me because it isn't what the room was actually worth. Jensen Huang, Sam Altman, Alexandr Wang, Boris Cherny, list goes on, were all there and worth hearing, but you can watch a talk from anywhere a week later. What you can't get anywhere else is a few thousand people deep in something hard, standing close enough to run into each other. It's a serendipity machine. A machine like that only runs on real inputs. A scripted conversation of "What are you working on, how big is your team, who's backing you" and then the quiet math of whether to keep standing there- thats not real input. The best conversations I had happened at the very end, hours in, when everyone was too tired to keep it up. One person walked me through the part of their system they still hadn't figured out. Another turned into an argument about the economics of intelligence. One had nothing to do with startups at all, and that's the person I've actually kept talking to since. I keep thinking about why the tiredness helped. I don't think exhaustion makes people honest, exactly. I think it just makes the performance too expensive to keep up, and what was underneath had been the more interesting thing the whole time. It's expensive for the listener too. You can feel when someone is talking at their idea of you instead of to you. So what I'm taking home has nothing to do with who was on stage. Next time I'd rather skip that part and start where the good conversations started. Worst case you meet fewer people. Best case you actually meet them.

Artifacts is live in Lemma (YC F25) . Every agent has its own goals, edge cases, and ways of failing. Artifacts maintains a record of how yours is supposed to work from its prompts, traces, and the context only your team knows. As your agent changes, that record updates with it. Lemma uses it to decide what should surface as an issue, and every issue you validate or dismiss updates what it looks for next.
